abstract: This chapter theorizes social network sites (SNSs) as 'networked publics,' arguing that they function simultaneously as the spaces constructed through networked technologies and the imagined communities that emerge from the intersection of people, technology, and practice. boyd examines the structural properties (affordances) that distinguish networked publics from unmediated publics and analyzes the dynamics that arise from these affordances, drawing out implications for how people navigate social life online.
key_claims: Social network sites are best understood as a genre of 'networked publics' rather than merely as technological tools.
Networked publics are shaped by distinctive structural affordances that alter the nature of public interaction compared to face-to-face publics.
These affordances produce predictable dynamics that participants must negotiate as they engage in social life on SNSs.
Understanding these properties has important implications for privacy, self-presentation, and social interaction in mediated environments.
methods: Conceptual and theoretical analysis synthesizing prior scholarship on publics, mediation, and social network sites.
Development of a framework distinguishing the technical/spatial and the social/community dimensions of networked publics.
Articulation of key affordances and their resulting social dynamics as an analytic lens.
findings: Networked publics are characterized by affordances such as persistence, replicability, scalability, and searchability of content.
These affordances give rise to dynamics including invisible audiences, collapsed contexts, and the blurring of public and private boundaries.
Participants develop strategies and social practices to manage the challenges introduced by these affordances.
contributions: Provides a widely adopted theoretical vocabulary (affordances and dynamics) for analyzing social network sites as networked publics.
Bridges media studies, sociology, and internet research by reframing SNSs within the longer tradition of theorizing publics.
Offers a framework applicable to questions of privacy, identity, and youth participation in mediated environments.
framing: The chapter situates itself within media and internet studies as well as sociological theory on publics and public life, extending the concept of publics into networked, technologically mediated contexts.
